notes.claim: HSE sets dead working as the normal policy. Live work is allowed only when dead working is unreasonable, live work is reasonable and suitable precautions are taken.
HSE recommends a sequence for dead working: identify the circuit, disconnect, secure the isolation, post notices, prove dead, and test the instrument before and after use.
Fault finding follows a logical approach and asks what events led to the fault. A visual inspection finds many faults that testing will not.
After a repair or modification the work is tested before the equipment is taken back into use, and a fault in a safety-critical function can stay hidden unless safety checks are made.
Half-splitting means measuring near the middle of the suspect path, so that whichever way the reading goes, about half of what is left is cleared.
For switches in series to a relay coil, one test in the middle of the run replaces testing each switch in turn. A good half is proved, and the next test halves what is left.
In a start/stop circuit the Stop is normally closed and the Start normally open and sprung. A normally open contact across Start keeps the coil fed once Start is released.
The normally closed Stop buttons and the overload contact sit in series with the coil, so opening any one interrupts the coil circuit. The coil is fed from one line and neutral, so 230 V.

HSE sets the order for dead working: identify the circuit, disconnect from every source, lock off, put up a notice, prove dead, and test the proving instrument before and after use. Labels are never assumed correct.

For low voltages, two-pole voltage detectors, test lamps or voltmeters with insulated probes and fused leads can be used to prove dead. Multimeters, which can be set to the wrong function, are not recommended.

HSE says work dead wherever possible, yet names tracing a malfunction in a control system as a case where dead working may not be feasible. Testing live conductors with an instrument is itself live work.
notes.contested: HSE says to work dead wherever possible, but its own guidance names fault-finding on a control system as a case where making it dead may be unreasonable. So live tracing is a judgement that needs its three conditions, not a habit.

notes.claim: Accidents often happen during fault-finding after a breakdown, when pressure to repair gets risks taken. Minor inconvenience from working dead will very rarely outweigh the risks of live work.

Open circuits and high resistance faults are found with a low resistance ohmmeter. A loose connection or mechanical stress can cause an open circuit, and loose connections or damaged conductors a high resistance fault.

A stop control must bring the equipment to a safe condition and takes priority over start controls. A normally closed Stop fails safe when a wire breaks, so a Stop that cannot stop the motor is serious.

Emergency shutdown systems and similar devices have to be maintained to do their job at all times. Where an unsafe situation cannot be repaired at once, isolate the affected area and disconnect where necessary.
A coil is made to close within a band of its rated control voltage. The standard gives 85% to 110%, and an undervoltage coil can chatter, fail to pull in at all, or burn out.
The coil voltage must match the supply, so a coil rated for a different voltage from its feed is a wrong part. A buzzing contactor can come from an incorrect coil among other causes.
A coil far below its rating may hum or chatter, or may not pull in at all, so the sign depends on the make. A buzz is one possible sign, not a certain one.
notes.contested: Sources describe low coil voltage as causing chatter or hum, or failure to pull in at all. None says which a coil at about 58% of its rating would do, so the lesson treats buzzing as one possible sign.

notes.claim: Re-energising safely means loads that could start unexpectedly are disconnected first. After a repair the whole function is tested before return to service, and one fault can mask another.
Start by asking what events led to the fault and by inspecting with the senses. Compressors, pumps and fans are typically controlled by direct-on-line starters.

A motor that loses one phase draws 173% of normal current in the other two. A fuse blowing or a protective device opening on one phase can cause it, and worn starter contacts are the most common cause.
A single-phased motor at rest produces no starting torque. It hums, may buzz or growl, and will not accelerate, because the rotating field collapses into a pulsing single-phase field.
An overload relay protects against sustained overcurrent, which a heavy mechanical load or bad bearings can cause. Set too low, it trips a healthy motor during normal running.
Measuring the current a motor draws needs the circuit energised and operating, which is live testing and needs the same judgement as in lesson 1.
Moisture is a frequent cause of earth faults when a motor sits idle in a humid place. An insulation test shows if the motor is wet or contaminated, or has a dead short to earth.

Published minimum insulation resistance values differ. One standard gives 1 megohm plus 1 megohm per kilovolt, one maker 5 megohms, and one training text 1 megohm as a line below which faults are likely.
notes.contested: Sources give different minimum insulation resistance values: IEEE 43 as quoted by one maker, a motor maker's 5 megohms, and 1 megohm as the usual shore line. Which applies depends on the insulation, voltage and maker.

notes.claim: An insulation resistance test cannot by itself confirm a motor is in good condition, because it does not test the entire insulation system.
On an insulated system a single earth fault does not interrupt the supply. It raises a warning, and the priority on board ship is to keep essential supplies running.
A second earth fault on another phase produces a short circuit current, so the first fault should be located and cleared at once.
With three earth lamps, a low resistance earth fault on one line makes its lamp dim or go out and the other two glow brighter. Lamps are not very sensitive to high resistance faults.

The faulted circuit can be found by opening breakers one at a time until the detector reads normal, closing each before opening the next. Breakers feeding vital auxiliaries are left until standby equipment is running.
The earth fault current is too small to operate conventional earth fault relays, so finding the fault is done by hand. Once found, the circuit is made dead before an insulation test.
A single earth fault doubles the electrical stress on the insulation of the other two phases, so even a tolerated fault is cleared quickly.

An insulated neutral keeps essential supplies running through a first earth fault. Marine high-voltage systems since the Second World War have generally earthed the neutral through a resistance instead.
notes.contested: Designers disagree on insulated against resistance-earthed neutrals: insulated keeps supplies running through a first fault but makes fault location manual, while resistance earthing allows automatic location. This describes general marine practice, not any navy.

notes.claim: A condition report code C1 means faults that are immediately dangerous and require action. The person ordering the work is told in writing, and where repair is impractical the operative isolates the affected area.
HSE advises dealing with the most important things first, such as those that could kill or seriously injure.

The goal of handover is accurate communication of task-relevant information across shift changes. Many accidents have occurred through failed communication at handover, mostly during planned maintenance.
If a job cannot be finished in one shift it is left in a safe state, with clear instructions for the next shift.
Accidents often occur during fault-finding when pressure to repair gets risks taken, so a safe fault-finding procedure is planned ahead.
One fault can mask another, so after a repair the whole function is tested before the job is called done.
